title: Human-in-the-Loop & Approvals
summary: Some actions are too risky or irreversible to let an agent take on its own. Human-in-the-loop puts a person in the path of those actions: the agent proposes, the action is held in an approval queue, and it only executes after a human signs off. The craft is knowing which actions to gate, keeping the pause auditable and resumable, and tuning the gate so you get safety without drowning humans in trivial confirmations.

subtopics.title: Why gate: some actions can't be undone
subtopics.explanation: An agent that reasons well 99% of the time still takes a catastrophic action 1% of the time, and if that action is irreversible — a payment, a mass email, a production deletion — that 1% is unacceptable. Gating inserts a human decision precisely at the boundary where a mistake becomes permanent. This is the entire justification for human-in-the-loop: you accept a little latency to make the worst outcomes impossible without consent.

subtopics.title: Reversible vs irreversible is the deciding line
subtopics.explanation: The single most useful question when deciding whether to gate is 'can this be cheaply undone?' A read, a draft, or a staged change can be reverted, so it rarely needs a human; a wire transfer or an irreversible API call cannot, so it does. Classifying actions along the reversibility axis — not just 'important' vs 'unimportant' — is what lets you gate the few actions that truly matter and leave the rest autonomous.

subtopics.title: The approval queue holds the proposed action
subtopics.explanation: When an agent hits a gated action it does not execute; it enqueues a structured proposal — action, arguments, reasoning, and a status — into an approval queue that a human reviews. The queue decouples the agent's proposal from the human's decision, so the two don't have to happen in the same instant. This queue is the concrete data structure that turns 'a human should approve this' into an auditable, inspectable workflow.
subtopics.example:
queue = []

def propose(action: str, args: dict, reason: str) -> int:
    item = {"id": len(queue), "action": action, "args": args,
            "reason": reason, "status": "pending"}
    queue.append(item)             # nothing runs yet
    return item["id"]

req_id = propose("issue_refund", {"order": "A-9", "usd": 40},
                 reason="customer reported double charge")
# a reviewer will later approve/deny queue[req_id]

subtopics.title: Pause the agent, then resume on the decision
subtopics.explanation: A gated action pauses the agent's run: its state is checkpointed, control returns to a human, and the loop only continues once a decision arrives — approved actions execute, denied ones feed a rejection back so the agent can replan. Because approvals can take minutes or days, the pause has to be durable, not a blocking sleep that ties up a worker. Making the loop cleanly pausable and resumable is what lets human review coexist with an otherwise autonomous agent.

subtopics.title: Balance autonomy against approval fatigue
subtopics.explanation: Gate too little and a rogue action slips through; gate too much and humans rubber-stamp everything, which is no safety at all. The tuning levers are risk tiers, thresholds (amount, scope), trusted allowlists for known-safe cases, and batching related requests so a reviewer decides once instead of fifty times. Getting this balance right is the difference between a gate that genuinely protects and a gate that trains humans to click 'approve' without reading.

foundations.overview: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is a safety pattern for agents that can take consequential actions in the world. Instead of letting the agent execute every tool call autonomously, you classify actions by risk — chiefly by whether a mistake is reversible — and route the risky, irreversible ones through an approval gate. On hitting a gated action, the agent enqueues a structured proposal (action, arguments, reasoning) into an approval queue and pauses; a human reviews the queue and approves or denies; the agent then resumes, executing approved actions and replanning around denied ones. Because approvals can be slow, the pause must be durable and non-blocking rather than a held thread. The final and hardest part is tuning the gate with risk tiers, thresholds, trusted allowlists, and batching so it stops genuinely dangerous actions without generating so many trivial confirmations that reviewers stop reading. Done well, HITL lets an agent stay largely autonomous while making its worst possible outcomes impossible without human consent.
foundations.formalDefinition: Human-in-the-loop is an execution pattern in which designated agent actions are not performed directly but are enqueued as approval requests that a human must accept before execution; the agent's control loop suspends its state at the gate and resumes on the human's decision, executing approved requests and treating denials as feedback for replanning.
foundations.whyItMatters: Autonomy and irreversibility are a dangerous combination: an agent operating on untrusted inputs will occasionally choose a wrong action, and if that action can't be undone the cost is unbounded. HITL is the control that caps that tail risk, and it is often what makes it acceptable to deploy an agent against production systems, real money, or external communications at all.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the agent as a capable junior employee with a company card. For everyday reversible tasks they act freely, but for anything that spends money, sends something you can't recall, or destroys data, they fill out a request slip and drop it in the manager's tray. The manager signs or rejects it, and only then does the action happen — the slip and the tray are the approval queue.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Requiring approval before an agent issues a refund above a threshold, sends an email to a customer, merges a pull request, executes a database migration, deploys to production, or spends beyond a budget — while letting it read, draft, search, and stage changes freely.
commonUseCases: Approval before payments, refunds, or spend above a threshold
Confirmation before destructive or production-changing actions
Manual review of low-confidence or high-impact agent decisions

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the agent is good enough, you don't need human approval.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Even a 99%-reliable agent takes a catastrophic action occasionally, and untrusted inputs make that likelier. For irreversible actions, the acceptable error rate is effectively zero, which only a human gate provides.
Over-gating floods reviewers, who then rubber-stamp approvals without reading — worse than no gate. You gate the few irreversible/high-cost actions and let reversible ones run autonomously.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An approval pause is just a sleep() until the human clicks.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Approvals can take minutes or days, so blocking a worker is wasteful and fragile. The pause must checkpoint state durably and resume on an event, not hold a thread.

interactiveExamples.explanation: The agent proposes a gated action into a queue and pauses instead of executing; a human later approves or denies, and resume() runs approved actions or returns a denial the agent can replan around. Nothing risky runs without a recorded decision.

checkpoints.prompt: Which property most strongly indicates an agent action should require human approval?
options: It takes more than one tool call
It is irreversible or hard to undo
checkpoints.explanation: Reversibility is the deciding line. Irreversible actions (payments, sends, deletions, deploys) make a mistake permanent, so they warrant a human gate; cheaply-undoable actions usually don't.

checkpoints.prompt: This approval gate is supposed to pause the agent, but it never actually blocks execution. What's wrong?
options: The tool runs unconditionally after proposing, so the gate enqueues a request but never withholds execution
checkpoints.explanation: The function enqueues a proposal but then falls through to run_tool for every action, so gated actions execute immediately anyway. A real gate must return/pause without executing until a human approves.

theory.question: How do you decide which agent actions should require human approval?
theory.directAnswer: Classify actions primarily by reversibility and cost: irreversible or hard-to-undo actions (payments, sends, deletions, deploys) and high-cost or high-scope actions get gated, while cheaply reversible ones (reads, drafts, staged changes) run autonomously. You refine with risk tiers, amount/scope thresholds, and trusted allowlists so the gate catches what matters without flooding reviewers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: It's a risk-based routing decision that maps each tool action to 'auto-run' or 'require approval' based on how bad and how permanent a wrong choice would be.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Autonomy plus irreversibility is dangerous — an agent on untrusted inputs will occasionally act wrongly, and for permanent actions the acceptable error rate is near zero, which only a human can provide.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You tag actions with a risk tier and reversibility flag, add thresholds (e.g. amount > $100) and trusted allowlists for known-safe low-value cases, and default unknown actions to 'approve'; risky matches enqueue an approval request instead of executing.

theory.whyImportant: It's the tuning that determines whether the gate genuinely protects you or just trains reviewers to rubber-stamp everything.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent auto-issues refunds under $25 for trusted accounts but queues any refund above that or any account deletion for a human, keeping the queue small enough that reviewers actually read each request.

followUps.question: What should the default be for an unknown action?
followUps.answer: Treat it as high-risk and require approval; fail closed so a newly added tool can't silently bypass the gate before it's classified.

followUps.question: How do you avoid approval fatigue?
followUps.answer: Use thresholds and trusted allowlists to auto-run genuinely safe cases, and batch related requests so a reviewer decides once instead of many times.

theory.question: How should an agent pause for approval and resume afterward, given approvals can take minutes or days?
theory.directAnswer: The agent enqueues a structured proposal and suspends by checkpointing its state durably — not by blocking a thread — then resumes on an approval event: approved requests execute, denials are fed back as feedback so the agent can replan. The queue decouples proposal from decision so the two needn't happen at the same moment.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A durable pause/resume mechanism where a gated action becomes a persisted approval request and the agent loop yields control until a decision arrives.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Human review latency is unbounded; a blocking sleep would tie up workers, break on restarts, and lose state, so the pause must survive time and process boundaries.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On a gated action, persist the proposal (action, args, reasoning, status) and the agent's resumable state, return control, and on an approve/deny event reload the state and either run the tool with the approved args or inject a denial message for replanning.

theory.whyImportant: It's what lets slow human review coexist with an otherwise autonomous, resource-efficient agent rather than pinning a worker per pending request.
theory.realWorldExample: An agent proposing a production deploy checkpoints its plan and pauses; two hours later an on-call engineer approves in a dashboard, an event resumes the run, and the deploy executes with the exact approved arguments.

followUps.question: What should a denial do?
followUps.answer: Feed the denial (and any reviewer note) back to the agent as an observation so it can replan or ask for clarification, rather than silently dropping the task.

followUps.question: Why persist the proposal's arguments explicitly?
followUps.answer: So the executed action is exactly what the human approved; re-deriving arguments after resume risks running something different from what was reviewed.

scenario.question: Your finance-ops agent auto-approved a $9,000 vendor payment that turned out to be triggered by a spoofed invoice email. Leadership wants approvals added without slowing routine work to a crawl. How do you design the human-in-the-loop layer?
scenario.directAnswer: Gate irreversible money-movement by risk tier and threshold: auto-run only trusted, low-value, reversible actions; queue any payment above a threshold, any new payee, and anything derived from external/untrusted content for human approval with the full proposal and reasoning shown. Make the pause durable, feed denials back for replanning, and batch routine low-value items so reviewers focus on the risky few.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A targeted HITL redesign that gates the specific high-cost, irreversible path that failed while keeping routine reversible work autonomous.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The agent had authority to move money based on untrusted input with no human checkpoint, so a single spoofed email caused an irreversible loss.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Tag payments as irreversible, require approval above a dollar threshold and for any first-time payee, flag actions whose arguments trace to external email as elevated-risk, enqueue a proposal with the invoice source and reasoning, and resume only on explicit approval; auto-run only pre-approved recurring low-value payments.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows applying the gate precisely where irreversibility and untrusted input meet, rather than either leaving the agent unchecked or gating everything into uselessness.
scenario.realWorldExample: After the change, payments over $500 or to new payees queued for approval; the next spoofed invoice surfaced as a pending request an approver rejected, while thousands of small recurring payments still cleared automatically.

followUps.question: Why specifically flag actions derived from external content?
followUps.answer: Untrusted inputs are the injection surface; elevating anything whose arguments come from an email or web page catches manipulated actions even when the dollar amount looks ordinary.

followUps.question: How do you keep reviewers from fatiguing on the new queue?
followUps.answer: Auto-clear trusted recurring low-value payments, batch similar requests, and surface only the anomalies (new payee, high amount, external source) for human eyes.

keyTakeaways: Human-in-the-loop puts a person in the path of risky actions: the agent proposes, a human approves, and only then does it execute.
Gate by reversibility and cost — irreversible or high-cost actions (payments, sends, deletions, deploys) need a human; cheap reversible ones don't.
Use an approval queue to hold a structured proposal (action, args, reasoning, status) so proposal and decision are decoupled and auditable.
Pause durably and resume on the decision: execute approved actions with the exact approved arguments, and feed denials back so the agent replans.
Tune the gate with tiers, thresholds, trusted allowlists, and batching so it stops what matters without causing approval fatigue and rubber-stamping.
